flashcards.a: A behavioral pattern that provides a way to access the elements of a collection sequentially without exposing the collection's underlying representation.

flashcards.q: What are the four participants in the Iterator pattern?
flashcards.a: 1) Aggregate (createIterator), 2) ConcreteAggregate (holds data, creates iterator), 3) Iterator (next, hasNext, current), 4) ConcreteIterator (traversal logic).
The client controls the loop by calling next() and hasNext(); classic Iterator pattern.
The collection controls the loop; client passes a callback (e.g. forEach(item => ...)); client doesn't call next().

flashcards.q: When should you use the Iterator pattern?
flashcards.a: When you need to traverse a collection without exposing its structure, want multiple independent traversals, or have non-trivial structures (trees, graphs).

flashcards.q: How does Iterator support multiple traversals?
flashcards.a: Each call to createIterator() returns a new iterator with its own position; several loops can run over the same collection independently.
Collections (list, set, map), trees/graphs (pre-order, BFS, DFS), lazy sequences/generators, pagination.

flashcards.q: How does Iterator relate to Composite?
flashcards.a: Composite trees are often traversed with iterators (e.g. depth-first or breadth-first iterator) so clients don't walk the tree manually.
Another name for the Iterator pattern (cursor = current position in the collection).

flashcards.q: Why might modification during iteration be forbidden?
flashcards.a: To keep behavior predictable and avoid subtle bugs; many implementations throw or behave undefined if the collection is modified while iterating.
A new Iterator (or ConcreteIterator) over that aggregate, so the client can traverse without touching the aggregate's internals.
Next element is computed only when next() is called (e.g. generators, lazy streams, filtered/mapped views), instead of building a full list upfront.

flashcards.q: How does Iterator differ from Visitor?
flashcards.a: Iterator only provides traversal (next, current). Visitor adds operations over a structure; you can combine them (iterate and visit each element).
When the collection is a simple array and you only need one direct loop; language's built-in for-of or forEach may be enough.

flashcards.q: What is a common iterator interface?
flashcards.a: next() (advance and return current or { value, done }), hasNext() or isDone(), and current() or currentItem(); many languages standardize this (e.g. Iterable protocol).
